messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 45
- Gender: Female
- Ethnicity: South Asian
- Relationship Status: Single
- Occupation: Plumber
- Trauma Type: Life-threatening illness
- Pcl5: 69

# The Weight of What She Almost Lost

Priya is forty-five years old, a licensed plumber who has spent the better part of two decades crawling beneath houses, threading pipe through tight spaces, and solving problems with her hands. She is the kind of woman who has always prided herself on being capable — on knowing exactly what to do when something breaks. That self-understanding began to fracture three years ago, when she was diagnosed with acute myeloid leukemia.

The diagnosis came quickly and without warning. One week she was bidding a commercial job; the next she was sitting in a hematologist's office being told that without immediate chemotherapy, she would likely be dead within months. She remembers the fluorescent lighting in that room with unusual precision — the slight flicker of one bulb near the window. She remembers the doctor's mouth moving and hearing almost nothing. She drove herself home, sat in the driveway for two hours, and did not go inside.

The months that followed were brutal in ways she had not anticipated. The chemotherapy left her unable to walk to the bathroom unassisted. She developed a serious infection that required an intensive care stay, and there was a night — she knows this because a nurse told her afterward — when her family was called in. She has no memory of that night, and the blankness of it frightens her more than anything she can consciously recall. It is a hole in herself she cannot account for.

Priya achieved remission fourteen months ago. By most measures, she is a success story. She has returned to work, resumed her contracts, and rebuilt much of her physical strength. But she moves through her recovery as though the illness is still somewhere close behind her, just outside her field of vision. She sleeps poorly, rarely more than four hours at a stretch, and when she does sleep she often wakes with her heart pounding, certain in the first disoriented seconds that she is back in the hospital bed, that the beeping she hears is a cardiac monitor rather than a truck reversing on her street.

At work, the smell of certain industrial cleaners — something about the chemical sharpness of them — stops her cold. Her hands go still on whatever she is holding. She has learned to step outside and stand in the air until the feeling passes, telling her apprentice she needs to check something in the van. She does not explain. She has not told anyone at work about the leukemia, and she intends to keep it that way. Illness, in her understanding of herself, is not something she is permitted to have been.

Her relationship with her own body has become uneasy and adversarial. She monitors herself constantly — a bruise, a patch of fatigue, a lymph node she thinks she can feel — and each small irregularity ignites a cascade of certainty that the cancer has returned. She cancels follow-up appointments and then reschedules them, caught between the need to know and the terror of finding out. She has not opened several letters from her oncology team.

The social world she once inhabited has narrowed considerably. She was never someone who leaned heavily on others, but she had friendships, a regular Sunday call with her mother in Mississauga, a colleague she used to meet for lunch. Those connections have thinned. She finds it difficult to be around people who speak casually about the future — plans for next summer, mortgages, retirement — as though time is simply available, as though it can be assumed. She knows something they do not, and the knowing separates her.

What she describes most quietly, almost reluctantly, is the sense that she did not come all the way back. That some part of her remained in that hospital room, in that night she cannot remember. She is present in her life — working, eating, paying her bills — but she watches herself do these things from a slight distance, as though she is not entirely convinced she survived.
